items.title: The Midterm Turnout Puzzle: Who Actually Votes When the White House Isn't on the Ballot
items.body:
Every four years, American politics seems to take over everything. Campaign ads, debates, and dinner-table arguments all revolve around one race. Two years later, the energy fades. The offices at stake are still important: all 435 House seats, about a third of the Senate, dozens of governorships, and thousands of state legislative seats. Yet far fewer people turn out to choose them.

This gap between presidential and midterm participation is one of the most reliable patterns in U.S. elections. It also shapes which candidates win, which issues get attention, and how each party plans its campaigns.

## How Big Is the Gap?

In recent decades, turnout in midterm elections has usually run well below turnout in presidential years. Typically, somewhere around 40 to 50 percent of eligible voters cast ballots in a midterm, compared with roughly 55 to 66 percent in a presidential election.

The 2018 and 2022 midterms were notable exceptions to the long-running trend of low participation. Both drew historically high turnout for a midterm, with 2018 reaching about 50 percent of eligible voters, the highest rate in roughly a century. Even so, those elections still fell short of the presidential contests that bracketed them. The "drop-off" between presidential and midterm years has narrowed in some cases, but it has not disappeared.

## Who Shows Up

Midterm electorates are not just smaller versions of presidential electorates. They differ in composition.

**Older voters are overrepresented.** Voting rates rise steadily with age. Adults over 65 vote at much higher rates than adults under 30 in every election, but the difference widens in midterm years. In a presidential year, a surge of younger and first-time voters partly offsets this imbalance. In a midterm, that surge is smaller.

**Habitual and partisan voters dominate.** People who vote in every election, including low-profile ones, tend to be more politically engaged and more strongly attached to a party. Occasional voters, who often decide to participate only when a presidential race raises the stakes, are more likely to sit out.

**Education and income matter.** Voters with college degrees and higher household incomes participate at higher rates than others, and these differences also grow in midterm years. Homeowners and people who have lived in the same community for a long time are likewise more likely to vote than renters and recent movers.

## Who Stays Home

The people most likely to skip a midterm include younger adults, newly registered voters, those with lower incomes, and those with less connection to local community institutions. Surveys regularly find several reasons:

- **Low awareness.** Many people simply don't know a midterm is happening, or know little about the candidates on the ballot.
- **Practical barriers.** Work schedules, caregiving duties, transportation, and registration deadlines can all make voting harder, especially when it feels less urgent.
- **Lower perceived stakes.** Without a presidential contest, some people feel their vote matters less, even though many of the decisions that most directly affect daily life are made by state and local officials.
- **Disillusionment.** Some non-voters say they feel neither party speaks to them.

## Why the Gap Matters Politically

Because the midterm electorate is older, more engaged, and more partisan, campaign strategy changes. Candidates and party organizations focus less on persuading undecided voters and more on motivating their committed supporters to show up. A party whose supporters are enthusiastic can benefit from a strong turnout of its base even if its overall support is no larger than the other side's.

The president's party also has a well-documented disadvantage. In most midterm elections since the end of World War II, the party holding the White House has lost seats in the House of Representatives. Political scientists offer several explanations: voters who are dissatisfied with the current administration may be more motivated to vote than those who are content, and the presidential "coattails" that help candidates in a presidential year are absent.

Turnout is not the only factor. Economic conditions, the president's approval rating, redistricting, candidate quality, and the national mood all play major roles. Studies have also found that high turnout does not always favor one party. The effect depends on which groups are mobilized in a given year and place.

## Closing the Gap

Election administrators, civic groups, and campaigns have tried many approaches to boost participation in off-year elections:

- Early voting, mail voting, and extended hours to give voters more flexibility
- Automatic or same-day voter registration in some states
- Nonpartisan outreach that explains what offices are on the ballot and what they do
- Reminders and community-based efforts to reach first-time and infrequent voters

Research suggests that simple, personal contact, such as a neighbor or volunteer encouraging someone to vote, can make a measurable difference. The effects are modest per person, but they add up in close races.

## The Takeaway

The midterm turnout puzzle comes down to a basic fact: the people who decide midterm elections are not a perfect mirror of the country. Those who vote are older, more partisan, and more consistently engaged than those who don't. That reality affects campaign messaging, party fortunes, and ultimately the policies that follow.

For voters, the lesson is simple. Elections with lower turnout give each individual ballot more weight. For anyone curious about how their community is represented, checking registration status, learning what's on the ballot, and making a plan to vote are practical first steps. Election dates, polling places, and deadlines can be confirmed through your state or local election office.

*This article is for general informational purposes and does not endorse any candidate or party. Turnout figures are approximate and vary by source and year.*
